subject: Banking
title: Interest Rate Decisions
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Interest Rate Decisions.

hook.text: Eight times a year, the Fed meets to decide interest rates. Markets move billions on every word of the announcement.

buildup.text: The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed controls this rate directly.

discovery.text: When the Fed changes this rate, every other rate follows: mortgages, car loans, credit cards, and savings accounts.

twist.text: The Fed doesn't set rates by law. It uses open market operations to push the rate where it wants.

climax.text: One number set eight times a year controls the cost of money for the entire economy. That's extraordinary power.

punchline.text: Eight meetings, one rate. It controls the cost of borrowing for everyone.

quiz.question: How often does the Fed meet to set interest rates?

details.summary: Central banks set benchmark interest rates by assessing inflation, employment, growth, and financial conditions. These decisions ripple through the entire economy, affecting everything from mortgage rates to stock prices within hours.
details.whyItMatters: Interest rate decisions are arguably the most consequential economic policy actions in the modern world. A quarter-point change can shift trillions in asset values and alter borrowing costs for millions.
takeaways: The Fed meets eight times per year to decide on rates
Decisions are based on inflation, employment, and economic outlook data
Markets often price in expected changes before announcements

faq.question: How far in advance do markets predict rate decisions?
faq.answer: Federal funds futures markets price in expected rate changes weeks to months ahead. By meeting day, the actual decision is often already reflected in market prices. Surprises cause the biggest market reactions.

faq.question: Why do small rate changes matter so much?
faq.answer: Even a quarter-point change compounds across trillions in loans, bonds, and derivatives. A 0.25% increase on $30 trillion in US debt adds $75 billion in annual interest costs, showing how small moves create massive economic effects.
